items.title: Medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round
items.claim: The idea that 'medieval people thought the Earth was flat' was popularised in the 19th century. Who is most responsible for spreading it?

options.text: Galileo, in his trial defence of 1633
Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which fabricated a debate at Salamanca about whether Columbus would sail off the edge
Karl Marx, as part of his critique of religion

items.reveal:
Bede (8th century), Aquinas (13th century), Dante (14th century) and the entire scholastic tradition assumed a spherical Earth — it was Aristotelian orthodoxy reinforced by Ptolemy. Columbus's argument with the Salamanca scholars was about the Earth's circumference, not its shape; they thought (correctly) it was too large to sail to Asia westward.

Washington Irving's 'A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (1828) was a partly fictionalised popular biography. It invented the flat-Earth debate to make Columbus look more visionary. The myth then became a stock anti-medieval, anti-Catholic talking point in the late 19th century (notably John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White).
items.why: Historiography matters. The 'Dark Ages' frame and the flat-Earth myth are products of later polemic, not medieval thought. The conflict-between-science-and-religion narrative is largely a 19th-century construction.

items.title: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991

options.text: After Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost reforms, the August 1991 hardline coup failed, Baltic states declared independence, Yeltsin took power in Russia; the USSR was formally dissolved by the Belavezha Accords (8 December) and Gorbachev's resignation (25 December); the Supreme Soviet voted itself out of existence on 26 December 1991
By a vote of all citizens in 1989

items.reveal:
Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary in March 1985. Perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness) loosened Soviet controls. Eastern European communism collapsed in 1989. The Baltic states declared independence in 1990-91.

The August 1991 coup by hardliners against Gorbachev failed within three days when Boris Yeltsin rallied resistance from a tank outside the Russian White House. Real power shifted from the USSR to Russia.

The Belavezha Accords (8 December 1991) saw the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declare the USSR dissolved. The Alma-Ata Protocol (21 December) added eight more republics. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December; the Supreme Soviet voted on 26 December.
items.why: The largest peaceful end of a superpower in history. The mechanism — internal reform, failed counter-coup, voluntary dissolution by republics — has shaped how subsequent transitions have been imagined.

items.title: Constantinople fell to Ottoman cannons in 1453

options.text: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople from 6 April; massive Hungarian-built cannons breached the Theodosian walls; the city fell on 29 May 1453, ending the 1,123-year Eastern Roman Empire

items.reveal:
Mehmed II, aged 21, had artillery cast by Orban, a Hungarian engineer — including the Basilic, around 8 metres long, firing stone balls of around 270 kg. The walls of Theodosius (built 5th century) had held for a thousand years; gunpowder ended their effectiveness.

Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died in the fighting; his body was never identified. Around 7,000 Byzantine and Genoese defenders faced perhaps 80,000-150,000 Ottoman troops.

Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque (it remained one until 1934, when Atatürk converted it to a museum; reconverted to a mosque in 2020). The fall pushed Greek scholars and texts west into Italy — fuel for the late Renaissance.
items.why: Military technology can end empires. The fall of Constantinople closes the medieval Mediterranean and marks a conventional boundary between medieval and early modern history.
